outcome: No proof, disproof, claimed proof or bound on whether there are infinitely many Newman-Shanks-Williams (NSW) primes has appeared since 26 January 2024. The only in-window material touching the question is a 2025 forum remark that treats the infinitude as a known conjecture, and a 2026 computation on a different Erdős problem (#383) with an AI disclosure; no source names an AI system in connection with the NSW infinitude question. nothing_found is false only because older and neighbouring events are recorded as discounted events below; none of them is in the window and none settles or moves the question.
problem_asks: Single question: are there infinitely many NSW primes? Parts: (1) the set of NSW primes, i.e. the primes among the NSW numbers, is infinite (equivalently, infinitely many members of the NSW family are prime). The bullet itself does not define NSW primes. The definition used here is taken from the live Wikipedia article 'Newman-Shanks-Williams prime': the NSW numbers S satisfy S_0 = S_1 = 1 and S_n = 2S_(n-1) + S_(n-2), with closed form S_(2m+1) = ((1+√2)^(2m+1) + (1-√2)^(2m+1))/2, and an NSW prime is a prime of that form. The bullet asks for nothing else (no bound, no density, no index set stated). Caveat: the definition is from the live article, not the frozen January 2024 wording, which I could not check.

events.what_happened: Newman, Shanks and Williams introduce the NSW numbers and NSW primes in 'Simple groups of square order and an interesting sequence of primes', Acta Arithmetica 38(2), 129-140 (DOI 10.4064/aa-38-2-129-140). The Wikipedia article says the work arose from whether a finite simple group can have square order. The article body gives 1981 and its citation gives 1980; OEIS gives 'Acta Arith. 38 (1980/1981)'. I could not open the paper; what it contains is known here only from secondary pages (Wikipedia, OEIS references, MathWorld, Prime Glossary).
events.revisions: Journal year given as 1980 in citations and 1981 in the Wikipedia body; OEIS gives 1980/1981.
events.delivers: Defines the NSW numbers and NSW primes and lists the first few. According to the secondary sources read, it contains no statement about the infinitude of NSW primes; I could not confirm what, if anything, the paper says about infinitude.
events.remains: The whole question: whether there are infinitely many NSW primes.
events.directly_checkable: The first primes in the family (7, 41, 239, 9369319, 63018038201 at indices 3, 5, 7, 19, 29 under Wikipedia's indexing) can be checked by hand from the recurrence; this does not bear on infinitude.
events.direction: Neutral: definitional, no infinitude claim identified.

events.what_happened: Barcucci, Brunetti, Del Lungo and Del Ristoro, 'A combinatorial interpretation of the recurrence f(n+1) = 6f(n) - f(n-1)', Discrete Mathematics 190 (1998) 235-240 (DOI 10.1016/S0012-365X(98)80008-3). Per search-snippet reports of Sellers's paper (not opened), the note closes by asking (1) whether there are infinitely many f_n that are prime and (2) whether there are infinitely many that are composite. I did not open the 1998 paper or the Sellers PDF, so the wording of question (1) is secondhand. A University of Siena repository abstract (snippet only) says the paper answers a problem of Bonin et al. (1993) on a combinatorial interpretation of the NSW recurrence.
events.delivers: Poses the question of infinitely many prime f_n (secondhand report). Delivers no answer to it.
events.time_since_posted: about 28 years with no answer found in these searches
events.direction: Neutral: poses the question. The composite half of the question was answered later (see sellers-williams-composite-2002); the prime half was not answered in any source I found.

events.what_happened: James A. Sellers and Hugh C. Williams, 'On the infinitude of composite NSW numbers'. The main theorem is that f_m divides f_((2m-1)n+m) for all m >= 1 and n >= 0 (stated for a generalised recurrence f_(n+1) = k f_n - f_(n-1), f_1 = 1, f_2 = k+1), which gives infinitely many composite NSW numbers. Sellers later gave a purely inductive proof in 'Infinitely many composite NSW numbers: an inductive proof', Missouri J. Math. Sci. 16(1) (2004) 20-23 (DOI 10.35834/2004/1601020); a University of Minnesota Duluth draft dated January 2003 has the same content (not compared). The OEIS entry A094666 (composite NSW numbers) links both papers. The 2002 date is my reading of the Fibonacci Quarterly volume 40(3); one snippet gave 2001, which is a PDF creation date, not a publication date. The PDFs were not readable in my fetch, so the theorem is taken from search-snippet summaries and should be read as secondhand.
events.revisions: Inductive proof: Missouri J. Math. Sci. 16(1) 2004, pp. 20-23; UMD draft January 2003. Fibonacci Quarterly year inferred from volume 40(3); not confirmed from the issue page.
events.delivers: Infinitely many composite NSW numbers. Restriction: the composite half of the Barcucci et al. question only. It establishes nothing about primes among the f_n.
events.remains: Whether infinitely many NSW numbers are prime: the whole problem.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal; James A. Sellers is a number theorist and Hugh C. Williams is a number theorist
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the composite-NSW paper (per search-result listing; the issue page was not opened)

checked_by.who: Missouri Journal of Mathematical Sciences editorial process
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the 2004 inductive proof (per search-result listing; not opened)

events.direction: Affirmative for composite NSW numbers. Orthogonal to the prime question: it answers a different question, which the problem does not ask.

events.what_happened: Andrew N. W. Hone, L. Edson Jeffery and Robert G. Selcoe, 'On a family of sequences related to Chebyshev polynomials', arXiv:1802.01793 (v1 6 Feb 2018; v3 23 Jul 2018); published Journal of Integer Sequences 21 (2018), Article 18.7.2. For a family of second-order linear recurrences (Lehmer-type, indexed by n), they prove that for one special class of n the sequence contains at most one prime, and conjecture that for all other n the sequence contains infinitely many primes, distributed like Mersenne primes among Mersenne numbers. The arXiv abstract I read does not mention NSW numbers. I read the arXiv abstract page only, not the full text or the JIS version.
events.delivers: For a special class of n, a finiteness dichotomy (at most one prime); for other n, a conjecture of infinitude only. It is about an analogous family, not NSW numbers, so it settles nothing about NSW primes.
events.remains: The NSW question in full. The family's infinitude conjecture for generic n remains a conjecture in the sources read.

checked_by.who: Journal of Integer Sequences editorial process
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper as Article 18.7.2 (listing seen in search results; the journal page was not opened)

events.direction: Neutral analogue: a conjecture of infinitude for other members of a different family.

events.what_happened: OEIS A330276 defines NSW pseudoprimes as odd composite k with A002315((k-1)/2) == 1 (mod k). Per that entry, Andrica and Bagdasar (2020-2022) conjectured the sequence is infinite, and 'their conjecture was proved by Grantham (2021)', citing J. Grantham, 'Proof of Two Conjectures of Andrica and Bagdasar', Integers 21 (2021), #A111. I did not locate the Integers paper. A Zenodo record with the same title is dated 19 Nov 2021, but its author field was blank in the page snippet I saw and I did not open it. Grantham's other infinitude results on Frobenius and Perrin pseudoprimes appeared in search snippets; they are about different sequences.
events.revisions: Zenodo record 19 Nov 2021 (snippet only, not opened).
events.delivers: Infinitely many NSW pseudoprimes (odd composite k satisfying the NSW congruence), as OEIS reports. A different object: the composite k in this result are not the NSW primes the problem asks about. Restriction: the result is as reported by OEIS; I did not read the proof.
events.remains: Infinitude of NSW primes: the whole problem.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (per OEIS reference; not verified in the journal)

events.direction: Affirmative for NSW pseudoprimes (a different family of composite numbers). Discounted for the prime question.

events.what_happened: Prime NSW indices (OEIS A005850, primes p with A002315((p-1)/2) prime) are extended by Eric W. Weisstein from p = 129127 up to p = 172243, between May 2006 and January 2007 (OEIS extension note; data from Mike Oakes, March 2009). The MathWorld table of largest known NSW primes gives the matching discoveries (index 64563 on 19 May 2006 through index 86121 on 25 Jan 2007, with index k corresponding to p = 2k+1). These are finite computational finds.
events.revisions: OEIS entry approved; extension dates from the OEIS note and MathWorld table.
events.delivers: Finitely many further NSW prime instances (p = 129127 to 172243). Finitely many instances of an infinitude question move nothing about infinitude.
events.directly_checkable: Primality of each NSW number is checkable by a standard primality test on the closed form; the OEIS entry marks some larger terms as probable primes only.
events.doubts: The OEIS entry says some larger terms may be probable primes only, not proven primes.

events.what_happened: Ray Chandler (Fort Worth, Texas) finds the 728-digit NSW number that PrimePages' curio page still calls the 'largest known' NSW prime, in September 2003. The curio page labels it a probable prime and was last modified 2 Mar 2024, with no new discovery recorded. By the digit relation (digits approximately n log10(1+√2) with n = 2k+1), this is prime index p of about 1901, which OEIS A005850 lists. The 'largest' label is therefore stale: larger NSW primes are listed elsewhere (see disputes and price-2018-index-139160).
events.revisions: PrimePages curio page last modified 2024-03-02 (edit, not a new discovery).
events.delivers: One finite NSW prime instance (probable prime, 728 digits). Does not bear on infinitude.
events.doubts: Probable prime only, per the curio page; the page says it has not been re-proven there.

events.what_happened: R. Price finds an NSW prime at MathWorld index 139160, with 106,535 decimal digits, recorded on 7 Dec 2018 in MathWorld's table of largest known NSW primes. Under the index convention k with prime index p = 2k+1, this is p = 278321 (my calculation; the digit count matches n log10(1+√2) with n = 278321). The OEIS list A005850 does not include this index: its last visible term is 172243. The table as I read it does not state the primality status of this entry.
events.delivers: One finite NSW prime instance, larger than the others listed. Does not bear on infinitude.
events.doubts: Primality status not shown in the MathWorld table as read; if it is a probable prime, it is a PRP record like the others.

events.what_happened: On the erdosproblems.com forum thread for Problem #383 (largest prime divisor of the product of p^2+i, i = 0..k, equals p), user Dogmachine (8 Sep 2025) writes that the first nontrivial case could be handled conditionally, 'by invoking the well known conjecture that there are arbitrarily many Newman-Shanks-Williams primes', and asks whether an unconditional proof of that case is known. The thread's only NSW mention per the page read; the site notes that comments are not verified for correctness. The remark is about #383, not about NSW primes.
events.delivers: Nothing about NSW primes. A conditional remark on a different problem, and a status signal: the NSW infinitude is referred to as a conjecture, not a theorem.
events.time_since_posted: about 13 months (as of October 2026); no reply to the NSW point found on the page
events.direction: Treats the NSW infinitude as a known, unproved conjecture. No result either way.

events.what_happened: On the same #383 thread, KentaKitamura (21 Jun 2026) posts a computation: the prime p = 9188057 satisfies the #383 condition for every k from 0 to 10, with search counts for primes up to 10^7 and none found for k = 11 to 15. The post discloses AI use: per my fetch summary of the page, it names Codex 5.5 (xhigh reasoning) and ChatGPT 5.5 Pro as helping with the computation and the comment. I did not obtain the verbatim sentence, so the disclosure is a summary, not a quote. The post concerns Problem #383, not NSW primes; it contains no NSW result.
events.delivers: Finite witnesses for the #383 condition at fixed k (one prime per finite k). Restriction: a finite check on a different problem; says nothing about NSW primes.
events.directly_checkable: The witness p = 9188057 can be checked against the #383 condition by hand or with a computer algebra system.
events.direction: Finite instances of a different problem. No bearing on the NSW question.

disputes.summary: Largest known NSW prime. The PrimePages curio page (last modified 2 Mar 2024) still calls the 728-digit Chandler 2003 probable prime the largest known NSW prime. A PrimePages entry for V(2,-1,9679)/2 lists 3705 decimal digits (PRP), seen in a search snippet and not opened. MathWorld's table lists index 139160 with 106,535 digits (R. Price, 7 Dec 2018). Using digits ≈ n log10(1+√2) with n = 2k+1 gives n ≈ 1901, 9679 and 278321 respectively, so the curio's 'largest' label is stale. This is a record-keeping conflict only; it does not bear on infinitude, and no in-window record was found.

The year of the Newman-Shanks-Williams paper is given as 1980 in citations and as 1981 in the Wikipedia body and some secondary pages (OEIS gives 1980/1981). Recorded as 1980 under the first public written argument rule; the discrepancy does not affect the window.

summary: Nothing in the window moves the question whether there are infinitely many NSW primes. I found no paper, preprint, forum post, lab announcement, or formal proof dated after 26 January 2024 that proves, disproves or bounds the question, and no source names an AI system in connection with it. The live Wikipedia article says nothing about infinitude beyond listing the problem in the unsolved-problems category; the OEIS entries for the primes and indices (A005850, A088165), the NSW numbers (A002315), the composite NSW numbers (A094666), and the related sequences A263429 and A099088 contain no conjecture about the infinitude of NSW primes. The in-window material touching the question is (a) a 8 Sep 2025 forum remark on Erdős #383 that cites 'the well known conjecture that there are arbitrarily many Newman-Shanks-Williams primes' as a status signal, and (b) a 21 Jun 2026 computation on #383 with an AI disclosure (Codex 5.5, ChatGPT 5.5 Pro, per a page summary; not verbatim), which concerns a different question. Older work is recorded as discounted events: the 1998 question (secondhand, the Barcucci et al. note, not opened); Sellers and Williams on composite NSW numbers (2002, with the 2004 inductive proof), which answers the composite half only; Hone, Jeffery and Selcoe (2018), a conjecture for an analogous Lehmer-type family; Grantham (2021) on NSW pseudoprimes, as reported by OEIS A330276, a different object; and finite prime records (2003, 2006-07, 2018), which are finite instances. The OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv 2608.11941; 492 open OEIS conjectures attacked by language models, with a DeepMind AlphaProof Nexus paper in Science, 8 Oct 2026) was checked for NSW entries: none of A005850, A088165, A002315 or A094666 carries an open infinitude conjecture, and the visible parts of the OEIS Open folders contain no NSW-named file. I could not enumerate the full 492 list, so this is not a list-level check. Close calls: (1) the composite theorem could be read as partial progress on the 'NSW family', but the problem asks about primes and the result is pre-window; (2) the 2025 forum remark is recorded as a status signal, not weighed; (3) the Grantham result is written up by OEIS as settling 'the sequence', which is the pseudoprime sequence, so it is discounted for this problem; (4) the record disagreement on the largest known NSW prime is a record-keeping issue with no bearing on infinitude. The Wikipedia article's year (1980 vs 1981) is a date conflict, recorded in disputes. Evidence limits are listed in incomplete.
competing_reading: A reader could treat the 2025 forum remark and the 2026 AI-benchmark activity around OEIS conjectures as signs that the problem is live. Against that, neither contains a result on the infinitude of NSW primes: the forum remark presupposes the conjecture, and an NSW-index conjecture in the OEIS Open list would have to appear as a settled item, which I did not find in the entries read or the partial folder listings. A second reading would count the Sellers-Williams composite theorem as partial progress on the NSW family. That reading treats 'composite NSW numbers' as the same quantity as 'NSW primes', which the question does not ask, and the result is pre-window in any case.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The full list of 492 OEIS Open conjectures (the tadamcz.com/oeis-open results explorer, the epoch-research LeanOpenProblems-results data, or the complete formal-conjectures OEIS folder), checked for A005850, A088165, A002315, A094666 and A330276. (b) The full text of Barcucci et al. (1998) and Sellers and Williams (Fibonacci Quarterly 40(3)), to confirm the exact wording of the prime question and whether either paper gives a partial result. (c) A full-text arXiv search for 'Newman-Shanks-Williams' and 'NSW prime' from 26 January 2024 onward, which I did not run beyond web search. (d) The current status of the Erdős #383 thread and any later NSW remark on it. (e) The Grantham (2021) Integers paper, to confirm its scope against OEIS's description. (f) The primality status of the 2018 Price find in MathWorld's current table.

incomplete: (1) The 1998 Barcucci et al. paper and the Sellers and Williams PDFs were not readable here (one was binary; the other not opened), so the exact wording of the prime question is secondhand from search snippets. (2) The 1980 Newman-Shanks-Williams paper was not opened. (3) The Grantham (2021) Integers paper was not located; its description comes from OEIS A330276 only, and the Zenodo record was not opened. (4) The Hone et al. JIS version and full arXiv text were not read; only the abstract page. (5) The full 492-conjecture OEIS Open list was not enumerated: the explorer and the epoch repository gave no list, and the formal-conjectures OEIS folder and the AlphaProof OEIS folder were only partly visible. I therefore cannot rule out that an NSW-index conjecture is among the 492, though none of the NSW OEIS entries read carries an infinitude conjecture. (6) The AlphaProof Nexus Science paper is paywalled; not read. (7) The 2608.11941 full text was read only to 100,000 of 137,632 characters. (8) The Erdős #383 page content was read through a fetch summary, so the quoted NSW sentence is as the fetch returned it. (9) The AI disclosure in the 21 Jun 2026 #383 comment is a summary, not a verbatim quote. (10) The Price 2018 record's primality status was not shown in the MathWorld table read. (11) No arXiv search or Google Scholar search was run directly; search-engine results only. (12) The live Wikipedia article was read, not the frozen January 2024 revision.

judgement.why: No event addresses the infinitude of NSW primes. The 1980 paper and 1998 note define or pose the question (none). Sellers–Williams (composite NSW numbers), Grantham (NSW pseudoprimes) and Hone–Jeffery–Selcoe (analogous Lehmer-type family) answer different questions (variant). Record-prime finds are finite instances. Both in-window events are forum posts on Erdős #383: one merely cites the NSW infinitude as a conjecture (none), the other is a finite computation on a different problem (variant); its AI disclosure has empty ai.systems and concerns a different problem, so ai_role none.
judgement.doubts: Barcucci et al. and Sellers–Williams were not opened; Grantham's scope comes only from OEIS. None of this could change scope for the prime question. The full OEIS Open list was not enumerated, so an AI-settled NSW item cannot be strictly excluded, though no NSW OEIS entry carries an open infinitude conjecture.
